# Icechunk: a versioned store {#sec-icechunk}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/book.R")
```

[Icechunk](https://icechunk.io) puts a transaction log in front of Zarr:
snapshots, branches and tags, so a reader can pin a version and keep
reading it while writers move on. Chunks are found through the snapshot's
manifest, not by key, and a chunk can be native (stored in the
repository), inline, or virtual (a byte range of a file somewhere else).

In R, [tabularberg](https://github.com/hypertidy/tabularberg) wraps the
Icechunk Rust library, and zaro opens a repository as a store.

## Bluelink, under a seal

The Bluelink ocean reanalysis (BRAN) of @sec-virtual is also published as
an Icechunk repository on
[Source Cooperative](https://source.coop/ausantarctic/ausantarctic-scratch/bluelink),
built with [raad.virtualize](https://github.com/mdsumner/raad.virtualize).
It is one array per variable from 1993 on, and every chunk is a virtual
reference into the netCDF files on NCI's THREDDS server. The repository
(the manifests and the coordinates) is read from Source Cooperative; the
data comes from NCI.

```r
store <- zaro_icechunk("https://data.source.coop/ausantarctic/ausantarctic-scratch/bluelink/bluelink-daily-temp/icechunk",
                       authorize = "https://", direct = TRUE)
store@snapshot                 # the version this store is pinned to
temp <- zaro_array(store, "temp", cf = TRUE)
```

The question to put to it comes from IMOS animal tracking. Elephant seals
carry CTD tags: each dive is a temperature and salinity profile at one
place and time, a quarter of a million of them in the Southern Ocean
since 2004. To compare a dive with the model you want the model's profile
under it: every depth level at one cell on one day.

That is `temp[i, j, , t]`, and with one level per chunk it is 51 chunks.
The natural code is a loop over dives.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| file: scripts/06-icechunk.R
```

```{r}
res <- book_run("06-icechunk.R", live = TRUE)
book_table(res)
```

On stock R the loop is one request after another, 51 for each dive. With
the method each dive is one batch. The second row is the workaround a
careful user can write today: build the index matrix for every level of
every dive by hand, and R passes it through whole in both builds. It is
the fastest of the three, and it is also the code nobody writes first.
The third read, a few days around a dive, has no matrix-subscript
shortcut that is not more trouble than it is worth.

```{r}
book_elt(res)
```

::: {.callout-note}
The dives in this script are made up, on the Kerguelen plateau, until the
IMOS seal profile store is wired in to supply real ones. tabularberg needs
a Rust toolchain to build; the book image includes it unless built with
`WITH_ICECHUNK=false` (@sec-rebuild), and without it this chapter has no
table. Requests to THREDDS are capped at 4 at a time.
:::

## Why the batch matters more here

With a plain Zarr store a chunk's address is its key. With Icechunk each
chunk is looked up in a manifest, and a virtual chunk then points at
another host. A reader given the whole request resolves all the
references in one pass over the manifest and can group the fetches by
host. A reader given one element at a time does that lookup once per
chunk. The deeper the indirection, the more a store gains from being
asked once.
